one_line: Walkthrough of Agent OS for Claude Code and Cursor: base and tool installs, opinionated standards files, roadmap-driven builds, and spec/resume commands. Mostly one demo run; the 95% claim is unsupported.
summary: The presenter introduces Agent OS, a framework that layers persistent standards and a planning workflow onto coding agents such as Claude Code and Cursor. Setup is two steps: a base install that creates directories and default standards files, then a tool-specific install run inside the project directory, with both usable together in hybrid mode. The base standards (best practices, code style, tech stack) act as global preferences, and the presenter says they should be made opinionated and that the instructions folder is framework-owned and should not be edited. The workflow centers on a plan-product command that generates mission, tech stack and roadmap files, after which the agent works through roadmap items in order. New features are added with create-spec, existing codebases are brought in with analyze-product, and sessions are resumed with execute-task. In the demo the agent kept a pnpm preference from the start and applied a TweakCN theme in one pass through a custom ShadCN rule. The evidence is one demo run plus anecdote, and the "learns from its mistakes" and "replaces 95% of AI coding" claims are not demonstrated.

key_ideas.idea: Agent OS adds a standards and planning layer on top of coding agents
key_ideas.detail: Pitched as letting the agent code like the user and keep a memory of what works. The shown mechanism is static standards and rule files, not feedback-driven learning.

key_ideas.idea: Setup is a base install plus a per-tool install
key_ideas.detail: The base install in the project root creates directories and standard files. The tool install (Claude Code or Cursor) runs in the directory where the project is created. Running both gives a hybrid setup. The exact commands are shown on the site and not spoken.

key_ideas.idea: Base standards are global preferences for every project
key_ideas.detail: Three files: best practices (including team-specific rules), code style (naming and structure), and tech stack (defaults the user replaces). The instructions folder is the engine and should not be modified, per the presenter.

key_ideas.idea: Specificity of the base files drives output quality
key_ideas.detail: The presenter says to make the base files as opinionated as possible. The plan-product input should cover app description, key features, target users and tech stack, and the tech stack can be overridden per project.

key_ideas.idea: Plan-product produces a roadmap that drives the build loop
key_ideas.detail: The command generates mission, tech stack and roadmap files, then builds the scaffold. Asking what is next makes the agent read the roadmap and propose the next uncompleted feature.
The presenter told the agent to use pnpm instead of npm at the start, and it kept using pnpm throughout the build. This is a single-run anecdote.

key_ideas.idea: A custom rule routes component work through the ShadCN MCP server
key_ideas.detail: The rule says to call the ShadCN MCP server whenever components are referenced, fetch their docs and implement them. The presenter pasted a TweakCN theme and reports it was applied in one shot, while noting that such setups usually miss parts of a theme.

execute-task resumes from a previous session. analyze-product replaces plan-product for an existing codebase; the agent reads code, infrastructure, style and development phase before creating the Agent OS files.

techniques.name: Two-stage install
techniques.how: Run the base install command in the project root, which creates the base directories and standard files. Then run the tool-specific install (Claude Code or Cursor) in the directory where the new project is created. Run both for hybrid mode. Exact commands are on the site, not in the video.
techniques.when: Starting any new project with Agent OS, or adding it to a tool setup.

techniques.name: Edit the standards folder before the first plan
techniques.how: Open the base standards folder (path or cd command shown on screen). In best-practices add team rules. In code-style set file naming and structure. In tech-stack replace the default with your stack (the video uses Next.js) and set the package manager (pnpm instead of npm).
techniques.when: Once per machine or team, before planning the first product, so every project inherits the same preferences.

techniques.name: Plan-product prompt structure
techniques.how: Invoke the plan product command with: a description of the app, its key features, target users, and the tech stack (or say to use the defaults). State exclusions explicitly, for example no database or auth for now. The output is mission, tech stack and roadmap files plus an initial scaffold.
techniques.when: Greenfield projects, to get a roadmap the agent can follow step by step.

techniques.name: Roadmap-driven build loop
techniques.how: Ask the agent what is next. It reads the roadmap, suggests the next uncompleted feature, and can be told to build a group of items at once (the presenter asked for all medium-size features).
techniques.when: Continuing a project across several work sessions.

techniques.name: create-spec for new features
techniques.how: Describe the feature (the presenter gives auth, a database or other large features as examples) through the create spec command. It writes an implementation plan, then ask for implementation either step by step or in one pass, depending on complexity.
techniques.when: Adding a large feature to an existing Agent OS project.

techniques.name: Custom tool-routing rule for a component library
techniques.how: Write a project rule file that tells the agent to call an MCP documentation server (here the ShadCN MCP server) whenever a named component is referenced, to fetch its docs, and then to implement it. Paste the theme code from the theme site and ask for it to be applied. The rule file contents are not shown in full.
techniques.when: A component library that has an MCP docs server and that the agent tends to get wrong without docs.

techniques.name: Resume with execute-task
techniques.how: In a new session, invoke the execute task command to pick up from the previous session.
techniques.when: Returning to an Agent OS project after a break or a context reset.

techniques.name: Retrofit with analyze-product
techniques.how: In an existing codebase, use analyze product in place of plan product and say you want Agent OS installed. The agent inspects code, infrastructure, style and development phase, then creates the context files.
techniques.when: Adding Agent OS to a product that is already built.

techniques.name: Invoke rules by tool syntax
techniques.how: In Cursor, reference files and rules with the @ symbol. In Claude Code, the commands are invoked as slash commands. The presenter hopes a future version will use Claude Code custom agents.
techniques.when: Using the installed commands in either tool.

numbers.claim: Two supported tools at the time: Claude Code and Cursor. Both can be installed together (hybrid mode).
Three base standards files: best practices, code style, tech stack.
In the demo project there were five rules: four installed by default plus one custom ShadCN rule. The presenter first said four.
The video gives no benchmarks, costs, latencies or token counts. The title's 95% figure is not supported.

hot_takes: The title's claim that Agent OS replaces 95% of AI coding is not backed by anything in the video. The demo is one feature-build run.
The intro says the framework lets the agent learn from its mistakes. The shown mechanism is static standards and rule files, and no feedback loop is demonstrated.
The one-shot theme application is a single anecdote. The presenter himself says ShadCN MCP setups usually miss parts of a theme.
The presenter says modifying the instructions folder breaks the system, without showing it.
The install commands are not spoken, so the walkthrough cannot be reproduced from the video alone.
Quality is capped at 2: a hype title with thin substance, and about a quarter of the runtime goes to channel plugs and an outro.

relevance.why: Name collision: this is a different Agent OS (a spec-driven coding-agent framework), not our AgentOS infrastructure. The only overlap is a standards and roadmap layer for agents.
relevance.action: No change needed. If context files are reorganized, compare the standards-folder split (best practices, code style, tech stack) with how our project docs are organized.

relevance.why: Overlaps with ProsHarness's plan-first flow and checkpoint/resume. The roadmap with completed and uncompleted items plus execute-task acts as a resume point for a long run.
relevance.action: Compare ProsHarness checkpoint/resume with Agent OS's roadmap plus execute-task. Test whether a roadmap-style file with done/not-done items is a simple checkpoint format.
